payload.stem: A neutral metal sphere rests on an insulating stand. A positively charged rod is brought near the sphere without touching it. Which statement describes the final charge on the sphere and gives the best reason?

options.text: The sphere ends up positive, because charge from the rod moves onto the sphere as the rod approaches.
options.why: Believes that a rod that does not touch the sphere still transfers its own charge to it.

options.text: The sphere ends up negative, because the charge on the sphere that is the same sign as the rod's charge flowed to ground while the rod was nearby.
options.why: The rod repels like charge to the far side of the sphere; grounding lets it leave, so the sphere keeps an excess charge of the opposite sign.

options.text: The sphere ends up positive, because the charge opposite to the rod's charge flowed to ground.

options.text: The sphere ends up neutral, because grounding discharges the sphere completely.

payload.stem: A positive test charge is moved at constant speed along a path that lies entirely on one equipotential surface of an electrostatic field. Which statement about the work done by the electric force on the charge during the motion is correct and best justified?

options.text: The electric force does positive work along the equipotential, because the charge moves in the direction of the field's component along the path.
options.why: Believes the work is the field times the path length regardless of the direction of the force.

options.text: The electric force does zero work along the equipotential, because the force is perpendicular to the equipotential surface and so to each small displacement along it.
options.why: The work equals $-q\Delta V$, which is zero when the potential does not change.

options.text: The electric force does zero work only if the charge moves slowly, so that it has no kinetic energy.
options.why: Confuses zero work with zero kinetic energy.

options.text: The electric force does negative work along the equipotential, because the charge must be pushed against the field.
options.why: Assumes an external agent is always pushing against the field.

distractor_explanation.notes: The explanation covers each wrong option. The distractor 9.00R ("multiplies length by diameter factor") is not a realistic misconception. The distractor 3.00R is labeled "inversely proportional to length", but inverse proportionality would give 1/3, not 3. The rationale for 3.00R therefore does not match its value; 3 would come from R ∝ L with the diameter ignored. This mislabeled misconception is a defect.

payload.stem: A long straight wire carries a current that increases at a steady rate of $10\text{ A/s}$. options.why: Uses the field at the near side times the whole area.
Omits the factor $1/(2\pi)$.
Uses the field at the middle of the loop times the area.
$\Phi=\dfrac{\mu_0IL}{2\pi}\ln\dfrac{a+w}{a}$, so $\varepsilon=\dfrac{\mu_0L}{2\pi}\ln\dfrac{a+w}{a}\dfrac{dI}{dt}=0.659\,\mu\text{V}$.

payload.stem: A battery, a switch, a resistor and an ideal inductor form a series circuit. The switch has been closed for a long time. A second resistor is connected in parallel with the inductor, and then the switch is opened. Which statement about the current in the inductor just after the switch is opened is correct and best justified?

options.text: Immediately after the switch is opened, the current in the inductor drops to zero, because the battery no longer supplies the circuit.
options.why: Believes the current in an inductor can change instantly when the source is removed.

options.text: Immediately after the switch is opened, the current in the inductor is unchanged in size and direction, because the inductor's emf opposes the decrease in current and keeps it flowing through the resistor.
options.why: An inductor opposes a sudden change in its current; the energy stored in its field drives the current through the resistor.

options.text: Immediately after the switch is opened, the current in the inductor reverses direction, because the inductor's emf opposes the original current.
options.why: Thinks an inductor's emf reverses the current rather than opposing its decrease.

options.text: Immediately after the switch is opened, the current in the inductor doubles, because the inductor's emf adds to the battery's emf.
options.why: Believes the inductor adds to the battery emf when the circuit is opened.
